title: Function Overloading and Default Arguments
summary: **Overloading** gives several functions the same name with different parameters, and the compiler picks the best match for each call. **Default arguments** supply a value when the caller leaves a parameter out.
markdown:
## One name, several functions Two functions may share a name as long as their parameter lists differ. This is **overloading**. ```cpp #include int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; } int add(int a, int b, int c) { return a + b + c; } int main() { std::cout << add(1, 2) << '\n'; // the (int, int) version std::cout << add(1.5, 2.5) << '\n'; // the (double, double) version std::cout << add(1, 2, 3) << '\n'; // the three-parameter version return 0; } ``` The caller writes `add` and the compiler chooses. That choice is called **overload resolution**, and it happens entirely at compile time. ```mermaid flowchart LR C["add(1.5, 2.5)"] --> R{"Which version
fits best?"} R -->|"exact match: chosen"| D["double add(double, double)"] R -.->|"would need a conversion"| I["int add(int, int)"] R -.->|"wrong number of arguments"| T["int add(int, int, int)"] ``` ## How the compiler ranks the candidates For each argument, the compiler prefers the candidate that needs the least conversion. | Rank | Kind of match | Example | |---|---|---| | 1 (best) | Exact | `int` to `int` | | 2 | Promotion | `char` or `short` to `int`; `float` to `double` | | 3 | Standard conversion | `int` to `double`; `double` to `int` | | 4 | User-defined conversion | Conversions you define on classes (Milestone 6) | If two candidates are equally good, the call is **ambiguous** and does not compile: ```cpp void f(long value); void f(double value); f(5); // error: int to long and int to double are both rank 3 ``` Fix it by making the argument's type exact (`f(5L)` or `f(5.0)`) or by adding an `int` overload. ## What makes two overloads different? | The functions differ in | Allowed? | |---|---| | Number of parameters | Yes | | Types of parameters | Yes | | **Only** the return type | No | | Only the parameter names | No | The return type is not considered, because a call such as `add(1, 2);` gives the compiler no way to tell which result you wanted. ## Default arguments A parameter can name a value to use when the caller supplies none. ```cpp #include void printLine(int length = 20, char symbol = '-') { for (int i{ 0 }; i < length; ++i) { std::cout << symbol; } std::cout << '\n'; } int main() { printLine(); // 20 dashes printLine(5); // 5 dashes printLine(5, '*'); // 5 stars return 0; } ``` | Rule | Detail | |---|---| | Defaults go on the **right** | `void f(int a, int b = 2)` is fine. `void f(int a = 1, int b)` is not. | | Arguments fill from the left | You cannot skip `length` and give only `symbol`. | | State the default once | When a function has a declaration in a header, put the default there and not in the definition. | > [!warning] Overloads and defaults can collide > `void log(int level);` together with `void log(int level, int indent = 0);` makes `log(3)` ambiguous. Use one mechanism or the other for a given name. ## Forbidding an overload `= delete` declares that a particular overload must not be called. It is a precise way to block an unwanted conversion. ```cpp void printInt(int x); void printInt(char) = delete; void printInt(bool) = delete; printInt(5); // fine printInt('a'); // error: this overload is deleted ``` Without the deleted versions, `'a'` would be promoted to `int` and print as 97. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Can two functions differ only in their return type? - Yes, the compiler picks one from the type you store the result in + No, the compiler chooses an overload from the arguments alone - Yes, but only if one of them returns `void` - Only if they are in different files > Overload resolution looks only at the arguments, so the return type cannot tell two functions apart. ? Is `void f(int x = 1, int y);` valid? - Yes, `y` simply has no default - Yes, and calling `f()` uses 1 for both + No, defaulted parameters must come after the others > Defaults fill in from the right, so every parameter after one with a default must also have one. Write `void f(int y, int x = 1);`. ? What makes a call ambiguous? + Two or more overloads are equally good matches - No overload matches the arguments exactly - The function has default arguments - The overloads are declared in different orders > If one overload is a better match the compiler picks it. Ambiguity means two are tied, and the call is a compile error. ? What does `void print(bool) = delete;` achieve? - It removes every overload of `print` - It makes `print` return nothing when given a `bool` + Calling `print` with a `bool` becomes a compile error - It deletes `print` at the end of the program > A deleted overload still takes part in choosing, so a `bool` argument picks it and the call fails to compile, rather than quietly converting to `print(int)`. ```
ideas:
1. Overload `print` for `int`, `double`, `std::string_view` and `bool`, each printing a label such as `int: 5`.
2. Write `double area(double radius)` and `double area(double width, double height)`.
3. Write `void greet(std::string_view name = "friend", int times = 1)`.
